name: Presidential Elections
description: Iran’s presidential elections combine direct popular voting with constitutional eligibility requirements and institutional screening. The 2024 election illustrates both the importance of competition between approved candidates and the limits of the presidency within the wider political system.

seo.title: Presidential Elections in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s presidential voting rules, the 2024 runoff, participation, and the relationship between electoral choice and presidential authority.

content.heading: What voters elect
content.content:
Iran’s constitution provides for a directly elected president serving a four-year term, with only one immediately consecutive reelection permitted. An absolute majority is required; otherwise, the leading candidates proceed to a runoff the following Friday. The Guardian Council supervises the election. The president heads the executive, except in matters reserved to the Supreme Leader. Electing a president therefore does not transfer all state authority to the winner. [s1]

Participation arrangements are geographically flexible. International IDEA’s pre-election factsheet for the 2024 contest states that voters could present identity cards and vote anywhere, rather than being confined to an individually assigned polling location. It also records overseas voting and mobile voting arrangements, and identifies voting as voluntary. These are descriptions of that election’s arrangements, not instructions for a future voter. [s2]

content.heading: How the 2024 runoff worked
content.content:
The early election held on 28 June 2024 produced no majority winner. Four candidates participated, and Masoud Pezeshkian and Saeed Jalili advanced to the second round. Voting in the runoff took place on 5 July. Reporting the announced result, Reuters recorded 16,384,403 votes for Pezeshkian and 13,538,179 for Jalili, from 30,530,157 ballots counted. These are reported administrative totals, rather than the results of an independent ballot audit. [s3]

Pezeshkian brought experience in both parliament and government: he had served as a legislator, parliamentary deputy speaker, and health minister. His victory illustrates why an Iranian presidential contest cannot be understood solely as a contest between fixed political parties. The candidates’ public records, factional associations, and perceived differences in governing approach also matter. [s3][s4]

content.heading: Competition, participation, and institutional limits
content.content:
Radio Farda reported turnout of approximately 40 percent in the first round and 49.8 percent in the runoff. The increase accompanied a campaign effort to persuade first-round abstainers to participate. Pezeshkian’s supporters presented his candidacy as a way to resist a more restrictive governing approach, while Jalili’s supporters criticized his orientation toward engagement with Western countries. These were competing campaign arguments, not demonstrated forecasts of what either administration would accomplish. [s4]

The distinction between electoral competition and unrestricted political choice remains essential. The result changed who would lead the elected executive, but it did not remove the authority of the Supreme Leader. Radio Farda also reported the United States government’s criticism that the election was neither free nor fair; that assessment should be attributed to its speaker rather than presented as an election-administration finding. [s4]

For readers, the useful questions are separate: how the votes were counted, what choices reached the ballot, how many eligible voters participated, and what authority the winner could exercise. A result can establish the successful candidate without, by itself, establishing public approval of every institution or policy. [s1][s3][s4]

name: Parliamentary Elections
description: Iran elects its single-chamber parliament through a system classified as a two-round majority system by the Inter-Parliamentary Union. Candidate screening, factional competition, and unequal participation across places are central to understanding the parliamentary vote.

seo.title: Parliamentary Elections in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore elections to Iran’s Majles, including candidate screening, the 2024 results, factional politics, and outstanding questions about current electoral rules.

content.heading: Electing the Majles
content.content:
The Majles, formally the Islamic Consultative Assembly, is Iran’s national parliament. The Inter-Parliamentary Union classifies its structure as unicameral: there is one parliamentary chamber. Its electoral-system profile places elections in the plurality/majority family and identifies a two-round system. Voting is not compulsory. Those classifications provide an introduction, but they do not replace the detailed rules governing individual constituencies and the conditions for a runoff. [s1]

The constitution assigns supervision of parliamentary elections to the Guardian Council. This supervisory institution must be distinguished from parliament itself: voters select legislators, while another body exercises electoral oversight. [s2]

content.heading: Who can compete
content.content:
Candidate approval substantially shapes the field before voting begins. The House of Commons Library’s account of the 2024 elections describes the exclusion of many reformist and moderate candidates, including serving parliamentarians. It also explains that candidates commonly compete through groups and factions rather than through cohesive parties resembling those familiar to many international readers. Reformist and conservative labels describe broad tendencies; neither should be assumed to denote a single disciplined bloc. [s3]

The same briefing links restrictions on expression and association to limits on political participation. This matters when interpreting a result: the distribution of seats reflects competition among those permitted to stand, rather than a comprehensive test of every political position held in society. [s3]

content.heading: Reading the 2024 result
content.content:
The 2024 election renewed the full legislature, with 290 seats contested. IPU’s completed-election record reports 14 women elected and describes conservative, or principlist, candidates as the dominant force. It records turnout at approximately 41 percent and places the election against a background of economic difficulty, disqualifications, and boycott calls. These circumstances are relevant context, but they do not identify the individual motives of everyone who abstained. [s4]

The runoff strengthened conservative control, according to Associated Press reporting after the second round. AP also described the exclusion of reformist candidates as a major feature of the contest. Its account makes clear that a runoff can complete the allocation of parliamentary seats while leaving the broader restrictions on political competition intact. [s5]

National turnout also conceals geographic differences. The Commons Library identified Tehran and some Kurdish- and Baluch-populated areas among places with particularly low participation. A national percentage should consequently not be treated as a description of every locality. [s3]

For a careful reading, distinguish the electoral formula, the approved candidate field, the constituency results, and the eventual parliamentary factions. Each answers a different question about representation. The inspected evidence supports this account of the 2024 contest, but a complete current guide still requires verification of the consolidated election law and constituency-specific rules. [s1][s3][s4]

name: Local Council Elections
description: Iran’s city and village council elections provide a channel for local representation within a centrally supervised administrative system. The timetable for the seventh council elections became uncertain in 2026, making it essential to distinguish legal provisions, announced preparations, and completed voting.

seo.title: Local Council Elections in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s elected city and village councils, their relationship to local administration, and the unresolved timetable of the 2026 elections.

content.heading: What local elections represent
content.content:
Iran’s constitution places councils within the organization of local public affairs, including development, health, education, and welfare. It also preserves the authority of the central government. Local representation therefore operates inside a national administrative framework rather than establishing autonomous local sovereignty. [s1]

The first nationwide popular local council elections took place in 1999. A historical study published by Nabz-Iran describes how elected councils introduced a new relationship between residents and municipal leadership. It also identifies tensions among council members, mayors, and appointed officials. Those tensions help explain why winning a council seat and possessing the resources or authority to resolve local problems are different things. [s2]

content.heading: Councils, mayors, and electoral oversight
content.content:
The council-law compilation inspected for this page describes direct, secret voting for city and village councils. It assigns city councils a role in selecting mayors, with formal appointment involving national or provincial authorities. Council elections consequently should not be described as a general direct election of mayors. The law also distinguishes the Interior Ministry’s electoral responsibilities from the central supervisory structure associated with parliament. [s3]

Historically, local elections have connected municipal concerns with national politics. Nabz-Iran’s account contrasts reformist success in major cities in the first elections with stronger independent representation in rural areas. It also describes how conservative control of Tehran’s council provided the route to Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s selection as mayor. These examples show why results in the capital can have national significance, while also warning against treating Tehran as representative of every village or provincial city. [s2]

content.heading: The unsettled 2026 timetable
content.content:
The seventh council elections require particular caution. IranWire reported in August 2026 that voting originally scheduled for 1 May had been postponed and that a replacement date required authorization from the Supreme National Security Council. It also reported disagreement about that body’s authority to extend elected councils’ tenure. This establishes a reported institutional dispute; it does not establish a definitive legal resolution. [s4]

On 30 September, Tasnim reported Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni’s proposal to hold voting during the first half of Aban, an Iranian Solar Hijri month. Tasnim rendered the proposed window as 23 October–6 November 2026. The minister said equipment had been distributed and preparations supported fully electronic voting. These were official claims about readiness and a proposed period, not evidence that polling had taken place. [s5]

The inspected sources do not establish whether voting had occurred by the research cutoff of 26 October. No completed seventh-election result is therefore presented here. Before publication as a current election guide, the timetable, applicable voting formula, and implementation arrangements need confirmation from final legal instruments and election notices. [s3][s4][s5]
